Q: Couldn't find Danger zone when trying to delet a repo in github A:

  1. Select the Repository: First, navigate to your profile and click on the specific repository that you wish to delete.

  2. Open Settings: Once you are inside the repository, look at the top horizontal menu bar and click on the Settings tab.

  3. Check the Navigation Bar: On the left-hand side, you will see a navigation sidebar. Make sure you are currently in the General section (it is usually the default view) not code review limits.

  4. Identify the Sections: On the right side of the screen, you will see various headings such as Repository name (where you can Rename), Default branch, and Releases.

  5. Scroll to Danger Zone: Scroll all the way down to the very bottom of the General settings page. There, you will find a section highlighted in red called the Danger Zone.

  6. Trigger Deletion: Within the Danger Zone, click the button labeled Delete this repository.

  7. Confirm Intent and Copy Text: A confirmation prompt will appear asking if you are absolutely sure about this action. To proceed and unlock the "Delete" button (which is currently "off" or disabled), you will see a specific string of text (the repository's path) shown inside double quotes (""). You must copy and paste that exact text into the input field provided.

  8. Final Confirmation Step: After clicking the delete button, there is one final step to verify your identity. There are usually two methods available for this.

  9. Email Verification: One common method is receiving a verification code via your registered email address. Open your email, find the code sent by GitHub, type it into the verification box, and submit.

  10. Successful Deletion: Once the code is confirmed, the repository will be permanently deleted from your account.

Q: Why does deleting a property from a JavaScript object significantly degrade performance compared to setting it to undefined? A:

(V8 developer here.)

Observation: The access time for objB (after delete) is consistently 5x to 10x slower than objA.

I cannot reproduce that with the example code you've provided. On the contrary, I see accesses to objB being slightly faster (and they're both too fast to matter or be profiled). If you've used a different benchmark where you saw the results you're describing, please post that.

My hypothesis is that delete triggers a transition to Dictionary Mode (Hash Table),

Yes. However, so does adding 10,000 properties to an object. So in your example, both objA and objB are in dictionary mode.

which bypasses the optimized JIT access paths.

No, objects being in dictionary mode is entirely orthogonal to JIT optimizations.

Is this transition to Dictionary Mode permanent for the lifecycle of that object, or can V8 re-optimize it back to a Hidden Class if the object remains stable?

The transition is not permanent, objects can be transitioned back. V8 only very rarely does this though, because switching an object's mode is very expensive, so switching back and forth repeatedly would be detrimental to performance.

Why is there such a significant difference between delete and undefined if the final number of active keys is the same?

Magnitude, direction, and explanation of such a difference all depend on the scenario.

Dictionary mode is faster for both adding and deleting properties. If your code adds and deletes many properties of objects, switching the objects to dictionary mode is much faster than keeping them in struct-like mode.

If your code reads the same few object properties over and over again, then keeping the object in struct-like mode means that where to find these properties in the object can be cached, whereas an object in dictionary mode needs to perform a dictionary lookup every time, which is still a relatively fast operation but not quite as fast as reading from a cached offset.

If your code reads 5,000 different properties, then once again keeping the object in dictionary mode is (much!) faster, because 5,000 dictionary lookups are faster than caching the offsets of 5,000 struct-like-mode properties and then never using those cached values again.

Is there a modern V8 flag or internal tool (like --allow-natives-syntax) to confirm if an object has been "de-optimized" to a dictionary?

Yes, there is %HasFastProperties(obj), which requires --allow-natives-syntax.
Do note that "fast properties" is a misnomer, and dictionary-mode properties are not generally worse; they're better at different things. See this answer for more details.

"Deoptimization" means something very different (namely having to throw away optimized code because its assumptions are no longer valid). Please don't conflate that concept with object representations.

Q: Invalidating JSON Web Tokens A:

One compromise is to trust the client-side JWT for most actions, provided the signature validates the payload of course, and the JWT hasn't expired. However, for anything state changing and/or sensitive our code then checks a couple of revocation lists.

For example, say we have the JWT payload structured as follows:

{
  "sub": "1234567890",
  "name": "John Doe",
  "iat": 1744470846,
  "exp": 1744471846
  "sessionId": 1000000
}

sub is the ID of the John Doe user in our database. Say our users have an ID (sub) starting from 1 and incrementing for each new account. This shouldn't be an issue for spoofing, as JWTs are signed.

Similar for sessionId... sessions have a numeric ID starting from 1 and session spoofing is prevented via JWT signatures.

If this session is logged out by the user clicking the Log Out button then we insert 1000000 in our revocation table, and the application also takes the expiry from the JWT and inserts it into the same record:

Session    Expires
1000000    1744471846

If any non-sensitive actions are carried out (e.g. reading a page containing information available to all logged-in users), then the JWT and signature is validated to ensure that the user is authorised. e.g. high-level-dashboard.htm

If any sensitive/state-changing actions are requested by the session (tuned to the risk appetite of the application), for example if "John" is a privileged user and wants to add a new privileged account to the system, the application validates the JWT and signature first without any DB lookups, and then it checks to find out if the session ID from the JWT (1000000) is in our revocation table.

In this case it is, as the user explicitly logged out so we give out an Access Denied as an attacker had in fact captured their JWT and was trying to replay it. For arguments sake, say they ran some malware on the user's device which captured the JWT, but as the user logged out of your application in time, this has prevented the replayed JWT of having any impact on the security of your application.

All the attacker can do is read pages such as high-level-dashboard.htm as these do not check this revocation list.

If John changes their password we do the same, however we also issue a new JWT for the session that changed the password (if they were logged in), so the session is not kicked out as the new session will have a different session ID.

Of course for timed out sessions, the JWT expiry automatically takes care of replay attacks.

In a different scenario, if John Doe's account is compromised and an admin disables it then we record the account as being locked in our locked accounts table:

sub           Last Session    Date Time Added
1234567890    1000001         1744470946

Last Session refers to the highest session ID in our system when the account was locked. As our session IDs are an incremental auto-number, for any state-changing actions we can check to see if the ID of our user (sub 1234567890) has a session in their JWT < 1000001 and log the user out (i.e. don't accept their JWT and delete the cookie) if this is encountered on a sensitive or state-changing action.

So locking an account adds the entry to this table and prevents further logins, and unlocking an account allows new logins. The entry remains in this table which effectively prevents old sessions (which may be attacker controlled) from doing anything critical with the JWT.

Of course, when JWTs are refreshed, both tables would be checked.

Clean Up

A scheduled task can delete entries in the revocation table that have Expires < Now().

The locked account table is more tricky as we never know if there's any JWT out there that has a session ID less than the highest session ID at the time an account was locked. I guess for ultimate security you must retain this locked accounts table forever, but you can update the Last Session should a user's account be locked out again. If your JWT expiries are consistent you could delete the records from Date Time Added + Session Length or it might make sense to store this in the user record itself.

Following Standards

Rather than using sessionId, the JWT standard claim jti (JWT ID) could be used.

Q: How to list all tags available in Docker registry for given image name using Docker CLI? A:

Listing tags in a repository is documented in the OCI tag listing API which calls the /v2/<name>/tags/list endpoint and parses the JSON output. You can manually script this with commands like curl, but that has a few downsides, particularly authentication and pagination. Different registries implement pagination differently, potentially breaking scripts that believe they have received the full list when they've only seen the first page of results. And authentication has different implementations depending on whether the registry points you to a token server or request basic auth, and whether you have a login or attempt to anonymously access the registry.

My suggestion instead is to use any of the various tools that handle all of the complexity for you, including crane from Google, oras from Microsoft, skopeo from RedHat, and regctl from myself.

crane ls ubuntu

oras repo tags docker.io/library/ubuntu

skopeo list-tags docker://docker.io/library/ubuntu

regctl tag ls ubuntu
